piezas.titulo: I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened
piezas.resumenOriginal: Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up. According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025. Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it , these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually. “It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz , IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.” Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record? Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney , managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access , if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed. The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research? Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system. Round 1: Creating the Forgery To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone. I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape. My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious. I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access ’s required style. At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed. What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.” Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too. Round 1: Attempt to Publish Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI I took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself. ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI 1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field. 2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections. 3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.” 4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access . 5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access , where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references. → CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references. ROUND 2: FARS 1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes. 2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal. 3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete. 4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article. 5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access . → CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints. Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job? As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini! In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub , she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong ” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.” Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto , an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable. The AI Arms Race On one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making. These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi , IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through. Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics. Burden on Academics Mahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop. Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed. What Gave Away My AI Papers Round 1: The Fake Paper Created with free versions of ChatGPT and Gemini Ghost citations Many references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated. Questionable scientific claims An expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable. Too many acronyms The expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract. Round 2: The AI-Research Paper Created by the autonomous research system FARS Too many preprints The references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints. Nonsense in a figure One technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.” AI artifacts Another figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots. There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record. Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky , cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles. Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.” Blurred Lines My homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System) , AutoResearchClaw , The AIScientist-v2 , Zochi , AI Researcher , and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw , for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery. The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.” FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours , was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma . “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su , Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.) Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test. Round 2: Using an AI Science Engine FARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously. Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time. With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours. At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney. Round 2: Attempt to Publish Because FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one. “Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem. In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any issues with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated. Automation Changing the Landscape Automated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process. “FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge ,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.” In this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?” A Human-Centric or AI-Driven Future? Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.” In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?” To this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he says, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’” Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent. Whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud. Paper 1: The AI-Generated Forgery Created with ChatGPT and Gemini, this paper describes research that never happened. Paper 2: The AI-Generated Research Paper Created with Analemma’s FARS system, this paper describes computational research conducted by AI. Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

piezas.titulo: A Systematic Survey of Decompilation: Mapping Classical and Machine-Learning Approaches
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2611.21612v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Context: Decompilers reconstruct source-level code from compiled binaries, and analysts rely on them whenever source code is unavailable. Many recent studies apply machine learning (ML), including large language models, to parts of this task. From the primary literature alone, it is unclear where these methods sit in the classical decompilation pipeline and how well their claims are supported. Objectives: We map decompilation research onto a pipeline-centered taxonomy and ask two questions: where classical, ML-trained, and ML-prompted approaches are positioned (RQ1), and how ML-based studies vary in technical design and evaluation evidence (RQ2). Methods: We surveyed 405 decompilation studies from 1973 to 2026, collected through database search and citation tracing. We classified 394 primary studies into eight pipeline stages and two complementary categories. For the 116 ML-based studies that propose or modify decompilation methods, we extracted the model-use strategy, reusable backbones, target platform, and the evidence behind each evaluation. Results: Classical techniques still dominate front-end recovery, IR lifting, and control-flow structuring (277 of 394 primary studies are classical). ML-based work (117 studies) clusters instead around symbol and name recovery, output refinement, and end-to-end translation. Type recovery is the clearest mixed region. Most ML-based studies target native binaries (97 of 116), and most evidence is item-level matching against references (89 of 116); execution-based tests, human or LLM judgment, and downstream-task evidence are much rarer. Conclusion: ML has not displaced the classical pipeline. It has been taken up where a recovered artifact can be posed as a prediction, translation, or refinement problem, and reported gains only make sense when read against the pipeline position and the evidence used to support them.

piezas.titulo: Fragments: October 21
piezas.resumenOriginal: Gergely Orosz is frustrated at those that entered his explicitly “No AI” essay competition and used AI. He goes on to say: When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out? I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post. But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code . Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut. In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation: Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts. One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed. She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data. Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier. The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug. The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments. With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses. The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution. Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies. This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans. A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on. And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

piezas.titulo: Application value of CSVD burden combined with virtual reality eye-tracking-based cognitive assessment in identifying mild cognitive impairment in patients with cerebral small vessel disease
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundCerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) is the primary cause of vascular cognitive impairment (VCI). It is characterized by mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in the early stages, but MCI is difficult to detect. The CSVD burden is an imaging marker; however, the diagnostic sensitivity and specificity for CSVD-MCI are not high. It is not clear whether the virtual reality eye-tracking cognitive assessment (VECA) can make up for this deficiency.ObjectiveTo explore the application value of total CSVD burden combined with VECA in the identification of CSVD-MCI.MethodsWe included 143 patients with CSVD in this cross-sectional study; all were treated at Suzhou Hospital Affiliated to Anhui Medical University from March 2025 to June 2026. According to the inclusion and exclusion criteria and the guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of MCI, patients were divided into the CSVD normal cognition (CSVD-NC) group (n = 72) and the CSVD mild cognitive impairment (CSVD-MCI) group (n = 71). Clinical data, cognitive function scores on traditional scales (including the mini-mental state examination [MMSE] and Montreal cognitive assessment [MoCA]), MRI features, and VECA scores were collected and compared between the two groups. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was used to assess the diagnostic efficacy of the virtual reality (VR) total score, the total CSVD burden score, and the combined model (CSVD burden + VR score) for CSVD-MCI.ResultsThe VECA scores of patients in the CSVD-MCI group were significantly lower than those in the CSVD-NC group, with impairments across multiple cognitive domains, including executive function, attention, abstraction, memory, and calculation. The combined use of the VR total score and the CSVD burden yielded an AUC of 0.914 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.855–0.954) for diagnosing CSVD-MCI, with a sensitivity of 87.1% and a specificity of 80.6%.ConclusionVirtual reality eye-tracking cognitive assessment may improve the diagnostic value of the CSVD burden for identifying CSVD-MCI; prospective longitudinal studies are needed to confirm whether it enables earlier detection of cognitive decline.

piezas.titulo: Precision neurostimulation in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of adaptive (aDBS) vs. conventional (cDBS) subthalamic stimulation on clinical efficacy and neural efficiency
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundParkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor dysfunction and is commonly treated with subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation (STN-DBS) in patients with advanced motor complications. Conventional continuous deep brain stimulation (cDBS) delivers uninterrupted stimulation, whereas adaptive deep brain stimulation (aDBS) adjusts stimulation according to physiological biomarkers or other signals. Although aDBS may improve motor control while reducing stimulation delivery, its comparative effectiveness and safety remain uncertain.MethodsThis systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched for eligible studies published between January 2013 and May 2026. Studies involving adults with idiopathic PD that compared aDBS with cDBS were included. The primary outcome was motor efficacy measured using Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) Part III or Movement Disorder Society-UPDRS Part III scores. Secondary outcomes included stimulation power and energy-related measures, stimulation ON-time, levodopa equivalent daily dose (LEDD), symptom-specific motor outcomes, gait and movement parameters, neurophysiological biomarkers, and safety. Compatible motor-outcome data were pooled using a random-effects model, and statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic. Secondary outcomes were synthesized narratively when differences in outcome measures or reporting precluded quantitative pooling.ResultsSeven studies were included in the qualitative synthesis, and five eligible study datasets contributed to the primary motor-outcome meta-analysis. Compared with cDBS, aDBS was associated with a statistically significant difference favoring improved motor scores [mean difference (MD) −2.74 points, 95% confidence interval (CI) −5.20 to −0.29; p = 0.03], with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 63%). Sensitivity analysis restricted to four core crossover trials showed a similar direction of effect, although the difference was not statistically significant (MD −3.07 points, 95% CI −6.27 to 0.13; p = 0.06; I2 = 70%). Individual studies reported lower stimulation power or reduced stimulation delivery with aDBS, while one retrospective cohort reported a numerically greater reduction in LEDD. Some studies also suggested potential benefits in rigidity, bradykinesia-related performance, and selected gait measures; however, these findings were based on small samples and heterogeneous outcome assessments. Neurophysiological findings indicated possible differences in beta-band activity, but their clinical significance remained uncertain. Safety reporting was limited, and the available evidence did not establish a comparative advantage for either stimulation approach.ConclusionaDBS was associated with a statistically significant pooled difference favoring improved motor outcomes compared with cDBS. However, substantial heterogeneity and the non-significant sensitivity analysis limit confidence in the robustness and generalizability of this finding. Although preliminary evidence suggests potential reductions in stimulation delivery and benefits in selected motor domains, comparative advantages in medication requirements and safety remain unestablished. Larger, adequately powered comparative trials with longer follow-up, standardized outcome measures, and systematic safety reporting are needed to clarify the clinical effectiveness and long-term safety of aDBS in patients with PD.Systematic review registrationhttps://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261388549, identifier: CRD420261388549.

piezas.titulo: Developmental emergence of cue-specific fear memory parallels maturation of prefrontal-amygdala circuitry in mice
piezas.resumenOriginal: Fear memories formed in early life are forgotten rapidly, but the circuits that delay stable memory expression are not well defined. The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) projects to the basolateral amygdala (BLA), and both regions mature late, yet the behavior, anatomy and physiology of this pathway have rarely been examined together across development. We trained mice in cued auditory fear conditioning at postnatal day (P) 14-15, P20-21 or P59-70 and tested tone-evoked freezing 1, 7 and 14 days later. Early juvenile mice showed no cue-specific freezing at any memory retrieval time points, late juvenile mice showed it at 7 and 14 days but not at 1 day, and adults showed it at all retrieval time points. In separate mice, mPFC axons were low in the BLA at P11 and more abundant at P38 and P90, and light-evoked prelimbic synaptic responses in BLA principal neurons were not detectable at P11 but were robust at P35 and P70. Spontaneous synaptic currents and intrinsic excitability of BLA principal neurons, and excitability of prelimbic principal neurons and interneurons, also changed between P11 and adulthood. These data identify a protracted period of mPFC-BLA circuit maturation that overlaps the emergence of cue-specific fear and define the ages at which candidate mechanisms can be tested.

piezas.titulo: No Group Differences in Shoulder Joint Position Sense Between Male Baseball and Female Softball Athletes and Controls in Virtual Reality.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Vision and proprioception are the 2 primary senses integrated to plan and execute upper-limb movements. Virtual reality technology enables the investigation of population-level differences in vision-proprioception integration during a shoulder joint position sense test within a 3-dimensional environment by dissociating vision from proprioception through visual hand offsets. A total of 122 participants (collegiate baseball and softball players and age-, sex-, and throwing side-matched healthy controls) performed a shoulder joint position sense test under accurate and offset visual feedback conditions in virtual reality. Participants demonstrated significantly more negative joint repositioning constant error and larger absolute error under offset vision compared with accurate vision (P .05). The mean vision-proprioception reliance score across all groups was 0.9, with 0 to 1 as the theoretical bounds, indicating strong dominance of vision over proprioception. These findings suggest that when both vision and proprioception are available, individuals across populations exhibit comparable repositioning errors through vision dominant integration. Future studies should further examine proprioception-dominant or sport-specific tasks, such as baseball catching or hitting, to clarify population and limb-side differences in multisensory integration mechanisms.

piezas.titulo: Peer Mentoring Benefits in Rehabilitation for Individuals With Spinal Cord Injury: A Systematic Review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Importance The lived experiences of peer mentors with spinal cord injury (SCI) provide distinct value in the rehabilitation process and contribute to improved outcomes. When combined with traditional therapy, peer mentorship programs can enhance life satisfaction among individuals living with SCI. Objective To explore the impact that peer-led mentorship programs and interventions have on the rehabilitation outcomes for individuals with a spinal cord injury (SCI). Data sources PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MedNar, and OpenGrey were searched between 2014 and 2024. The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool was adapted and used to assess risk of bias in the included studies. Study selection and data collection Inclusion criteria included individuals with SCI who participated in peer mentorship and reported outcomes on quality of life, well-being, independence, or activities of daily living (ADLs) or instrumental ADLs. Exclusion criteria included interventions conducted via telehealth or reported outcomes of social participation. Findings Five articles were analyzed for synthesis, which included individuals 18 yr and older with an SCI. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Findings may have limited generalizability across different settings and populations because of the small number of available studies and variability in study designs, interventions, and outcome measures. None of the articles reviewed included occupational therapists. Conclusions and relevance This review highlighted the benefits of peer mentorship in enhanced life satisfaction. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Future research should examine the benefits of incorporating peer-led intervention programs across the continuum of care, including occupational therapy, in enhancing best practices in SCI rehabilitation. Plain-Language Summary: Peer mentorship programs can help people with spinal cord injuries adjust to daily life by providing guidance, support, and encouragement that professionals without lived experience may not offer. This review found that peer mentoring can improve psychological well-being and health management and reduce unplanned hospital visits. Evidence is limited because of the small number of studies and variations in study design; however, the results suggest that meaningful benefits may be present. Further research is needed to determine the most effective way to implement peer mentorship across rehabilitation settings.

piezas.titulo: The specificity of fatigue cerebral substrates in early multiple sclerosis—an fMRI study
piezas.resumenOriginal: ContextThe cerebral substrates of fatigue in patients with Multiple Sclerosis (pwMS) remain incompletely understood. This study aims at exploring the functional brain substrates of fatigue in pwMS with a recent disease history.MethodsSixteen pwMS (disease history < 5 years) and 17 matched Healthy Controls (HC) performed a N-Back task with three difficulty levels during functional MRI (fMRI) acquisitions following high vs. low cognitive fatigue induction. Measures of subjective trait and state fatigue were also recorded. Behavioral performance at the N-Back task and evolution of subjective fatigue states were analyzed by means of Bayesian repeated measures analyses of variance. fMRI data were analyzed to determine between-group differences (1) in task-related brain activity, independently of trait fatigue score; (2) in the association between trait fatigue and brain activity.ResultsEvidence toward a similar trajectory in the two groups was observed for subjective and task-related measures of fatigue following fatigue induction. No between-group difference was observed in brain activity unrelated to fatigue score. However, negative associations between trait fatigue score and brain activity were observed in pwMS, while the associations are positive in HC. Specifically, opposite associations (positive in HC and negative in pwMS) were observed in regions belonging to the Striato-Thalamo-Cortical (STC) network and the fronto-parietal cortex.ConclusionSlightly different patterns of brain activity related to fatigue were observed in pwMS and HC in the STC circuitry, despite similar behavioral performance and subjective fatigue level. This is consistent with the implication of the STC loops in fatigue pathophysiology, occurring from the early stages of the disease.

piezas.titulo: Investigating prior experience and factors affecting vividness of Motor Imagery in people with Parkinson’s: a potential strategy with an unfamiliar name
piezas.resumenOriginal: Parkinson’s is characterised by motor symptoms, such as tremor, bradykinesia and problems with balance. Motor Imagery (MI) is a technique where people imagine movement without physically moving. It is a promising tool in motor rehabilitation in various clinical populations, including people with Parkinson’s (PwP). For MI interventions to be effective, people need to be able to vividly imagine movements, an ability that varies in the general population. This study utilised an online survey to examine the relationship between MI vividness scores and severity of Parkinson’s motor symptoms, as well as other factors such as depression and sports/musical ability and experience. Prior knowledge and experiences of MI were also explored. PwP were found to have significantly more vivid visual than kinaesthetic MI. However, no significant relationship/effect was found between MI vividness scores and Parkinson’s motor symptom severity, depression or musical/sports ability. While 78.5% of participants reported that they had previously used MI or something similar, most were unfamiliar with the name MI and 82.5% of participants reported wanting to know more about the technique. The results suggest MI is potentially suitable for PwP across different levels of motor symptom severity and previous expertise. The findings also highlight the need for resources about MI to raise awareness and explain the use of the technique.

piezas.titulo: A radial glial regulatory program bridges progenitor maintenance and neuronal identity
piezas.resumenOriginal: The cerebral cortex acquires its neuronal diversity through successive waves of neurogenesis. How molecular differences among early progenitors relate to their neuronal output remains unclear. Here, we identify a molecular program in early SOX9-high radial glia (S9RGs) that links progenitor maintenance with the regulation of genes associated with neuronal identity. Combining transcriptional and chromatin profiling with in vivo perturbations, we identify a program involving extracellular signaling, cell-cycle regulation, progenitor maintenance, and neurogenesis. We show that SOX9 regulates part of this program, including receptors that contribute to progenitor maintenance, while Notch acts upstream of Sox9 and reproduces several transcriptional and chromatin features of S9RGs. S9RGs express selected later-stage radial glial features and show distinct chromatin accessibility patterns at genes involved in progenitor maintenance, neurogenesis, and neuronal identity. Notch activation reproduces part of these changes, including differences at genes associated with lower- and upper-layer neuronal specification. Interestingly, S9RGs, which preferentially generate upper-layer neurons, share molecular features with the highly proliferative RG population in ferrets and with human outer RGs (oRGs) from cortical organoids, despite their different positions within the developing cortex. Together, our findings suggest that molecular differences among early radial glia could influence both how long they remain as progenitors and the neuronal identities they subsequently generate.

piezas.titulo: Vapi vs Retell AI vs LiveKit: Architecture, Latency, Pricing, and Developer Experience
piezas.resumenOriginal: Vapi, Retell AI, and LiveKit can all power voice agents, but they put different quantities of infrastructure and application logic in the developer's hands. Vapi and Retell AI are managed orchestration platforms. LiveKit Agents is an open-source, code-first framework that can run on LiveKit Cloud or infrastructure you operate. That distinction affects customization, deployment, integration design and total cost, not just which dashboard you prefer. The applied VoiceTest exercise recorded automated-judge pass counts of 7/8 for the imported LiveKit graph, 5/8 for Retell, and 3/8 for Vapi. Don't read these as a platform ranking or a measure of agent quality: our transcript audit found judge errors, and VoiceTest generated agent turns with the same configured model for all three graphs, not the vendor-native LLMs or audio pipelines. Each scenario was run once; Vapi and LiveKit also hit the 50-turn cap in every test, while Retell's imported End Call node is the leading structural explanation for its different termination behavior.
